opening:
My 12-year-old loves pie. Not the filling — the crust. He has always been that kid who eats around the fruit and saves the pastry for last, like it is the point. So I stopped making full pies and started making him hand pies instead. All crust. Maximum crunch. A jammy little pocket of tropical fruit inside that he tolerates because it is surrounded by the thing he actually came for.

These are pineapple and pear, spiced with ginger and cloves, sealed inside a dough built to shatter. The secret is frozen butter grated straight into cold flour — not cut in, not rubbed in, grated — so the fat stays in thin ribbons that puff and crunch in a hot oven the way a full pie crust can only dream of.

These fruits have been on West African tables for generations — not as novelty, not as borrowed flavours, but as pantry staples. Pineapple sold at the side of the road in Ibadan, peeled and quartered and dusted with salt. Pear sliced into salads, pressed into juices. I put them in pastry at 4am and dusted them with snow, and they tasted exactly like a Sunday should.
heritageHeadline: The Fruit That Was Always Ours
heritageSubhead: Pineapple and pear didn't arrive at our table. They were already there.
heritage:
Before it was a pastry filling, it was breakfast in someone's compound in Lagos.

Pineapple has been cultivated across West and Central Africa since the 16th century, introduced through trade routes from South America and immediately absorbed into the fabric of daily life. By the time it reached colonial-era markets, it was already ours — sold by women at roadsides, pressed into drinks, sliced thick and handed to children as an afternoon snack. In Nigeria, pineapple is not an exotic ingredient. It is a staple. It is Tuesday.

African pear — the kind you find in Nigerian markets — is a different creature entirely from the European varieties that dominate American grocery shelves. Ube, as it is known in Igbo, has a buttery, avocado-rich flesh that softens in heat and carries a faint nuttiness that no canned pear can replicate. It is boiled in salted water and eaten alongside roasted corn. It is a food of community, of slowness, of sitting outside with people you love while something cooks.

When I built this filling, I wasn't reaching for West African flavour. I was reaching back to something that was already sitting there. Pineapple and pear together, spiced with ginger — the warming root that runs through so much of our cooking — and cloves, the spice that smells like harmattan and grandmothers and something you can't quite name.

What this recipe does is give those flavours a new architecture. The hand pie is not a Nigerian form — but the filling inside it is unmistakably West African in its bones. Ginger that blooms in the heat of the oven. Pineapple that breaks down into a jammy sweetness with a bright, acidic edge. A lime finish that lifts the whole thing and makes you reach for the next one before you've finished the first.
pullQuote: The best things you can put in a crust are the things that were already on your table before anyone told you they belonged there.
scienceHeadline: Why I Grate the Butter Instead of Cutting It In
science:
Most pie dough recipes tell you to cut cold butter into flour using a pastry cutter or your fingers — working it until you have pea-sized pieces. It works. But pea-sized pieces are still thick enough to create pockets of fat that melt unevenly in the oven, sometimes leaving you with a crust that is flaky in one bite and doughy in the next.

Grating frozen butter changes the equation entirely. Frozen butter on a box grater produces thin, even ribbons that distribute through the flour in a way no cutter can replicate. Those ribbons stay cold longer, coat more surface area, and create a more consistent lamination through the dough. When the oven heat hits them, each ribbon produces its own pocket of steam — and it is that steam, multiplied hundreds of times, that makes the crust shatter rather than bend.

Pastry flakiness is a function of fat distribution and water content. When butter melts in a hot oven, the water inside it — butter is roughly 15–18% water — turns to steam almost instantly. That steam pushes the layers of gluten-coated flour apart, creating the airy gaps we read as flake. The key is keeping the fat cold until the oven does its work.

The tectonic fold amplifies this effect. Folding the dough in thirds, rotating, and repeating creates dozens of thin layers — each one separated by a film of butter. This is the same principle behind laminated doughs like croissants and rough puff pastry, applied to a standard hand pie dough with a fraction of the effort.

The chilling window matters too. Two and a half hours minimum, not as an afterthought but as an active step. That rest allows the gluten to relax — making the dough easier to roll — and keeps the butter cold right up until it hits the oven. Skip it and you lose the crunch.

What you taste at the end is the payoff of temperature management. The outside shatters. The inside yields. The filling holds its shape because the *cornstarch* has thickened it into something stable, not wet.
closingLine: May your Sundays be loud with the sound of something good.
ingredients:
All-purpose flour — 420g
Unsalted butter, frozen and grated — 340g
Fine salt — 1 tsp
Granulated sugar — 1 tbsp
Ice water — 120–180ml
Canned pears, drained and diced small — 425g (15oz)
Canned pineapple, drained and diced small — 425g (15oz)
Brown sugar — 3 tbsp
Unsalted butter — 1 tbsp
Ground ginger — ½ tsp
Ground cloves — ¼ tsp
Fresh lime juice — 1 tbsp
Cornstarch — 1 tsp
Egg, for egg wash — 1 large
Powdered sugar, for dusting — to taste
method:
Grate the butter. Freeze your butter for at least 30 minutes — it must be completely solid. Using a box grater, grate the frozen butter directly into your flour, salt, and sugar. Toss lightly with a fork between handfuls to coat the ribbons in flour. Do not use your hands to rub the butter in — the heat of your palms will melt it. Toss only.
Hydrate and fold. Add ice water one tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork after each addition, until the dough just comes together when pressed — shaggy, not smooth. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Press the dough into a rough rectangle, fold it in thirds like a letter, rotate 90 degrees, fold again. Repeat twice more. The dough will look rough. That is correct.
Chill. Wrap the dough tightly and refrigerate for a minimum of 2.5 hours. Do not rush this. The rest relaxes the gluten and keeps the butter cold.
Make the filling. Dice pears and pineapple small — roughly 1cm pieces. Melt butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Add fruit, brown sugar, ginger, and cloves. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the liquid releases and then evaporates — about 8 minutes. Whisk cornstarch into lime juice and stir into the pan. Cook one more minute until thick and jammy. Refrigerate until completely cold. Cold filling is non-negotiable — warm filling will steam inside the pie and make the crust soggy from the inside.
Roll and cut. Preheat oven to 400°F (200°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment. Roll the dough to ⅛ inch thickness. Cut into rectangles approximately 4 × 5 inches — you will need pairs. Score a small vent pattern into the tops before assembly.
Fill and seal. Place a bottom rectangle on the baking sheet. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of cold filling into the centre, leaving a clear ½ inch border. Brush the border with egg wash. Press the top rectangle over firmly and crimp the edges with a fork to seal completely. Brush the top with egg wash. Any unsealed edge will burst open in the oven.
Bake. Bake at 400°F for 18–22 minutes until deep golden brown. The colour you want is amber, not pale gold — that deep colour is what tells you the crust has set and crunched through. Cool on the pan for 10 minutes before moving.
Dust and serve. Sift powdered sugar generously over the cooled pies. Serve warm or at room temperature. Best eaten the day they are baked — the crust is loudest fresh from the oven.
